question: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
base_frame:
Q: Describe a house at the end of a quiet street.
A:

steered.text:
It is the number three house, and the number is peeling, just like the paint on the shutters. The shutters are painted a sky-blue that has forgotten how to be blue, now a bruised purple, and they do not shut, they merely swing in the draft, listening to the wind.

The house sits alone, or so it thinks, because the street is so very quiet. It is a house built of grey stone, the kind of stone that drinks the rain and keeps the water in its belly. There is no moss on it, for the moss is a sign of age, and this house is young, though the roof tiles have dropped one by one, and I have heard them clatter like dead birds.

Inside, the floorboards sing when you walk, a low, moaning tune that you do not hear till the sun is up, till the sun is up and the window-panes are fogged with your breath. The window-panes are thick, the glass is old and green, and you cannot see the garden from here, no sir, you cannot see the garden from here, for the garden is a garden of weeds, and the weeds are tall as your father's knee, and the weeds are singing the same low, moaning tune.

Outside, the lamp-post leans, and the lamp-post is the only thing that stands straight, and it casts a shadow that looks like a man with a limp, and the man with the limp is the man who owns the house. He owns the house, but he owns the house only on Tuesdays, and on the other nights he sleeps in the cellar, for the cellar is dry, and the cellar is the only place in the whole wide world that is dry.

The house has a clock in the hall, a clock that ticks backwards, and the clock ticks backwards only when the moon is full, and the moon is full only when the moon is full, which is a lie, for the moon is never full, the moon is never full, and the moon is the eye of a god who doth blink, and the god doth blink and the house doth creak, and the house doth creak and the house doth scream.

plain.text:
At the very edge of the map, where the paved road yields to a narrow strip of overgrown wild grass, stands a house that seems to have forgotten how to hurry. It is a modest, two-story cottage with a roofline that dips and sways slightly, as if the builder had a gentle breeze in mind while laying the shingles. The paint, a soft, weathered sage green, has faded to a creamy yellow under decades of sun, peeling just enough to reveal the warm, raw wood beneath, giving the structure an honest, unpretentious character.

A wraparound porch, supported by columns that have been smoothed by countless hands, invites the eye to linger. Here, a single wicker chair sits angled toward the garden, cushioned by a patchwork quilt that speaks of seasons long passed. Vines of climbing jasmine have learned to scale the trellis, their white flowers exploding into the summer air with a scent that hangs heavy and sweet, masking the distant hum of the nearby highway.

The yard is not manicured but curated; a garden bed overflows with lavender and daylilies that spill over the garden wall, while a small, slightly crooked oak tree provides a dappled shade on the south side. The windows are framed in dark, polished mahogany, reflecting the slow passage of clouds rather than the frantic pace of the world beyond. Even the streetlamp at the corner casts a warm, amber glow that seems to belong only to this final stretch of quiet, turning the ordinary gravel driveway into a stage for the evening shadows. It feels less like a dwelling and more like a secret kept by the earth, waiting patiently for those who know how to listen.
